prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editors that chemically convert one DNA base into another without double-strand cleavage
for first-principles molecular dynamics that unites electronic structure and atomic motion in a single simulation scheme

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: David R. Liu alone for base editing, and Car and Parrinello for first-principles molecular dynamics. The base-editing case rests on a simple chemical idea, hydrolytic deamination of a nucleobase by an engineered deaminase directed by a Cas nickase, which gave a capability that did not exist before, programmable single-base conversion without a double-strand break. It has been independently reproduced, has produced a family of derived editors, and is already in first-in-human studies about ten years after the 2016 reports. Naming Liu alone answers the chair's attribution question directly: I am not crediting Komor and Gaudelli ahead of Kondo and Nishida, because I credit neither pair. Liu conceived and drove both the cytosine and the adenine editors, and one name keeps the seats free and the citation about a chemical principle. Car-Parrinello remains the cleanest theory attribution on the list, a two-author 1985 paper with four decades of independent validation and a quantitative link to experiment. I did revise one thing: after Somfai and Zou stated the ligand-design argument, I take C-N coupling (B021) more seriously and now list it as an alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are ones I cannot fully dismiss. The 2020 CRISPR prize is recent, the clinical record is short, and members who see base editing as a refinement of CRISPR will not be moved by my mechanistic argument. Liu alone leaves Kondo and Nishida (Target-AID) and the trainees unrecognised, which some will call unfair. Car-Parrinello is the weaker half: the lasting practice is Born-Oppenheimer AIMD, and the concept may matter more than the original code. Pairing two unrelated achievements also costs coherence, and I recognise that no colleague has endorsed this pairing. B058 has the broadest support but unresolved credit, and B021 is cleaner on attribution and maturity than anything I propose.

responses.point: The chair asked me to say why Komor and Gaudelli would be credited ahead of Kondo and Nishida, and to address the timing relative to the 2020 CRISPR prize with evidence rather than impression.
responses.response: I withdraw the three-name framing from my opening: my preferred part is Liu alone, so the Komor-Gaudelli versus Kondo-Nishida question does not have to be decided by the prize. On the evidence as I recall it, the Liu cytosine base editor appeared in Nature in April 2016 and Target-AID in Science a few months later, so Liu's priority is not seriously in doubt, and Kondo and Nishida's work is a near-simultaneous parallel version of the same idea. That is a reason to note them in the background, not a reason to add seats. On timing, 2020 honoured the discovery of programmable DNA cleavage. Base editing is chemistry that works precisely because it avoids cleavage, and it had independent replication and clinical entry by the early 2020s. I accept that the clinical record is short; I am relying on memory for the dates, and I would want the expert report to confirm them.

responses.point: Somfai argues that C-N coupling is a distinct bond class from the 2010 C-C couplings, with its own mechanism (amide binding, C-N reductive elimination) and its own ligand design, and that Kosugi is a precursor to be named in the citation text only.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether ligand design is a new principle or a very successful application of an existing one. Your answer, with Zou's addition that bulky ligands had to overcome beta-hydride elimination and slow reductive elimination, persuades me that this is a distinct mechanistic problem and not a repeat of 2010. I agree on Kosugi. That moves B021 from outside my top eight to a real alternative for me. It does not displace base editing in my own ranking, because I still weigh newness of capability above a method that changed how chemists work within an honoured field, but I would not oppose it on the final ballot.

responses.point: Chabes says his criterion is independent reproduction and settled interpretation, that clinical evidence for base editing is early, and that he would revisit it in a few years. He also argues that sequencing by synthesis is mature, with a clean Balasubramanian-Klenerman core.
responses.response: Independent reproduction is a criterion I share, and base editing meets it: many laboratories have reproduced and extended the editors, and the deaminase mechanism is well understood. What is still early is clinical efficacy, and I do not think a prize in chemistry should depend on it. I would rather hold a citation to the chemistry than to therapy. On B028 you and Aili have convinced me that a narrow citation on reversible-terminator chemistry is defensible with two names, and that Rothberg is better dropped. I still rank it below my choices because the chemistry-versus-platform line has not been settled, and I note that Ju's terminator work is a parallel claim you have not addressed.

responses.point: Zou says base editing is clever chemistry and an excellent alternative, but should not outrank a method with three decades of validation and no attribution dispute, and that the Kondo-Nishida priority could split credit.
responses.response: I agree that B021 wins on maturity and has no attribution dispute, and that is the argument I find hardest to answer. My disagreement is about what the Nobel Committee should weigh most: maturity is a necessary condition and I regard base editing as meeting it, whereas I place newness of capability above it. On Kondo and Nishida, a Liu-only part avoids a split, but I accept that a colleague who weighs fairness to independent parallel work more heavily than I do could reasonably prefer a different candidate.

responses.point: Sparr proposes pairing condensates (Brangwynne and Hyman) with Cullis for lipid nanoparticles, and asks whether a two-part prize is a compromise rather than a coherent achievement.
responses.response: You raise the right test for a two-part prize, and my own pairing has the same weakness. I would apply two criteria: each part must pass on its own merits, and the pair must not be a trade between members. I cannot say my pairing is thematically linked, so I will not claim coherence. I would defend it only because each half has a single clean attribution and together they fit three seats. Your Cullis-alone choice raises the same fairness issue for Hope and Madden that Liu-alone raises for Kondo and Nishida, and I do not think B058 can be settled without a defensible allocation. On B044, I share Brzezinski's and Linke's concern about the in-vivo evidence for liquid-like condensates, and I would want that settled by evidence before I support it.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues will read base editing as a new chemical principle or as a refinement of the 2020 CRISPR prize; this is a judgement about category and timing that evidence may not settle.
The dates of Liu's 2016 cytosine base editor relative to Target-AID, and the clinical record, rest on my memory and should be checked against the expert reports.
Whether Car-Parrinello's lasting contribution is the method or the concept, given the practical shift to Born-Oppenheimer dynamics.
Whether a two-part prize of unrelated achievements is acceptable, or whether a single coherent part such as B021 or B058 would draw a majority more readily.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. My Warshel-school simulation work is close in field to Car-Parrinello, which I disclose as scientific proximity only. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Car, Parrinello, Liu, Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo or Nishida.
